method: Written by Claude Opus 5.5 in a Claude Code session after reading every letter with text; not produced by the batch pipeline.
summary: Testimony on LD 1822 centered on its limits on collecting personal data, its restrictions on sensitive data, and how it compares with the privacy bills heard alongside it. Letters in support described protections for people at risk of surveillance or discrimination, while letters in opposition argued that it departs from other states and would restrict digital advertising; others asked for changes to enforcement, coverage and exemptions.

themes.label: Limits collection to what a requested service needs
themes.detail: Letters said LD 1822 lets companies collect only the personal data needed for the product or service a person asked for, instead of anything disclosed in a privacy policy or accepted by clicking "I agree". Several contrasted this with the notice-and-consent approach of the bills heard alongside it.

themes.label: Restricts and bans the sale of sensitive data
themes.detail: Letters supported allowing sensitive data such as health, location, biometric, sexual orientation, immigration status and minors' data to be used only when strictly necessary, banning its sale, and limiting geofencing around health care facilities.

themes.label: Protects people at risk of surveillance or discrimination
themes.detail: Letters described how the bill would protect patients seeking reproductive or gender-affirming care, LGBTQ+ people, survivors of domestic and sexual violence, immigrants, older adults, people with disabilities and people leaving prison, and supported its ban on discriminatory processing of personal data.

themes.label: Reduces harms from data brokers, breaches and government purchases
themes.detail: Letters cited scams, stalking, data breaches, individualized pricing, election manipulation, and police or federal agencies buying data without a warrant as harms that collecting and selling less data would reduce.

themes.label: Gives people rights to see, correct and delete their data
themes.detail: Letters pointed to the rights to confirm what is collected, access, correct and delete it, opt out of targeted advertising and sales, and obtain a list of the third parties a company sold the data to.

themes.label: Out of step with other states and untested
themes.detail: Letters argued that LD 1822 follows a Maryland model not yet in effect, departs from the framework adopted in neighboring and other states, and would raise compliance costs or leave Maine an outlier.

themes.label: Would limit targeted advertising that Maine businesses rely on
themes.detail: Letters from businesses and trade groups said the collection limits would effectively end personalized and targeted advertising and ad measurement, putting small businesses, tourism and retailers at a disadvantage against competitors elsewhere.

themes.label: Sensitive-data and minors' rules too rigid; consent preferred
themes.detail: Letters argued the "strictly necessary" standard and sale ban remove consumer choice and could block fraud prevention, emergency alerts or bank biometric security, that the sensitive-data definition is too broad, and that the "should have known" standard for minors is unclear.

themes.label: Add or keep exemptions and narrow specific requirements
themes.detail: Letters asked to exempt or keep exempting particular sectors and data, including financial institutions under federal law, insurers, auto dealers, fraud investigators, hospitals, medical device data, public records and nonprofits, and to raise thresholds, narrow the financial-data definition, and clarify loyalty program, third-party and assessment rules.

themes.label: Close gaps and extend coverage
themes.detail: Requests included applying data minimization to use and sharing, dropping entity-level exemptions for health care, higher education, nonprofits and financial institutions, requiring a universal opt-out signal, narrowing publicly available information and consent loopholes, covering bankruptcy sales, revisiting the knowledge standard for minors, and adding social care data as sensitive.

themes.label: Add a private right of action and fund enforcement
themes.detail: Letters asked for a private right of action, possibly with a cure period or small-business limits, or at least funding for the Attorney General to enforce the law, and asked that enforcement and outreach reach vulnerable consumers.

themes.label: Possible effects on law enforcement tools need review
themes.detail: The State Police said they were still reviewing the bill for effects on tools used to identify suspects and locate next of kin, including how its health-data definitions interact with required pharmacy reporting.
